FOREWORD This Indian Standard (First Revision) was adopled by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Documentation and Information Sectional Committee had been approved by the Management and Systems Division Council. Alphabetical arrangement means arrangement of letters or their combinations according to the traditional ordinal values of letters, which increase as we proceed from the first to the last letter of the alphabet. While usage fixes a unique arrangement among the letters of an alphabet, groups of letters with different spacing, punctuations and other marks and the introduction of alien characters, which cannot be avoided in any collection of entries, give rise to possibility for several alternative arrangements. This calls for standardization of alphabetical arrangement of entries. Such a standard is of vital importance not only to documentalists, bibliographers and librarians but also to users and producers of bibliographic, catalogues, indexes to books, directories, such as telephone directories and lists of similar nature, such as voters' lists. Since 1952, when the first edition of this standard appeared, there have been new developments in librarianship, documentation, publishing and allied fields and information retrieval system has become both manual and mechanical. Computer has come into the field. The arrangement of items of information and records is increasingly being achieved by automatic means. This implies that rules have to be framed that can be applied without much of intellectual judgement in obtaining the desired arrangement. The variations between the first edition and the present edition are to be found in the rules dealing with numerals and symbols, hyphens and apostrophes, groups of initials and complex entry elements. Thq first edition prescribed that all numerals and symbols should be arranged as if spelt out and thus interfiled alphabetically with other entries, the present edition prescribes the alternative of separate filing sequence for each category. The previous edition did not recognize the use of hyphen either in joining together two words join a prefix to a word. The presence of punctuation marks including hyphen is ignored. cannot be maintained with automatic filing by computer. The use of hyphen in either case is is the case with apostrophes. This standard maintains that phylians and apostrophes should be for filing purposes. or being used to This distinction dying out and so treated as spaces

Groups of initials have come into use with various forms. Their number has increased and there are now dictionaries for such groups of inf,ials even as acronyms. No specific rule has been prescribed in the previous editions. UNESCO or INSDOC, etc, does not specify when to treat the initials of a group as individual words and when to treat the group as a whole. Pronounce ability is a guide but it is always possible with certain group of initials like FID, which is called fid. The previous standard ignored their treatment. This standard prescribes those groups of initials, which should be taken as whole words unless they are written out with spaces between the component alphabets to be, treated as separate words. The elements of complex entries at times pose difficulties in filing. A rigorous alphabetical sequence is not possible particularly when the entries filed relate to various elements. They should be arranged in alphabetical sequence of their entry elements followed by the alphabetical arrangement of secondary, tertiary or subsidiary element.

Indian Standard

PRACTICE FOR ALPHABETICAL ARRANGEMENT ( First Revision)
1 SCOPE The rules contained in this standard concern alphabetical arrangement of entries in bibliographies, catalogues, indexes, directories and lists of similar nature. While they do not go into a detailed prescription of how entries should be written, recommendations regarding certain problems in the writing of entries have become unavoidable. It also provides guidance on the arrangement of entries not strictly alphabetical on the filing of numerals and symbols, and of complex entries. The standard does not prescribe rules for determining the form of entries nor for arranging words and initials in non-reman ulphabets. 2 .ARRANGEMENT 2.1 Basis The basis of arrangement shall be all-through alphabetization for words. The numerals and symbots sha[l have their own sequence if expressed in numerals. If they are given in words then they will form the alphabetical sequence. The sequence of entries shall be : First: Numerals Second: Symbols Third: Alphabets A-Z 2.2 Rules 2.2.1 Presence of space, punctuation marks, accents, apostrophes and brackets shall be ignored. Examples Powder Power Power, electric Power, francis fountain Powerful machine Power (Mechanics) Power of a lie Power-operated Power's handbook of engineers Power, Stephen Anderson Electrode boiler Electrode-holder Electrode, metal Electro-deposits Electrode R6cepteur Electrodes Electrode (Wire) 2.2.2 Differences in the style of writing letters including capital and small letters shall be ignored. Examples INDIA AND PAKISTAN Fiscal Agreement. India Associated Corporation Report. India. Banking. Hubback (J.A.). Indian Banking. INDIA. Despatch on proposals for constitutional India. Ed. Views of the recommendations Commission. India. History. Selvam (C.) History of India. India. Indian Fiscal Commission Report. India. Jt Auth. Indo-British treaty by Great Britain and India. local government of the Indian on the Statutory reforms. Ltd.

2.2.3 Abbreviations and contractions shall be arranged according to the way they are written and not according to the words for which they stand. Examples a) Saint Andrew Sainte-Beuve, Cherles Augustin Saint Helana SH Sq cm St Cyr Ste Anne

IS 382:2003 St George Taper pins T Bars, Steel Tea Chests Teak Scantlings Tea Powder Tech Bull Tea Bars Tea Steel Tee Bars, Steel Tee Slots Tee Squares Tots T Slots T Squares Other Lunguuge Entries 3 NUMERALS 3.1 Numerals shall be arranged in a separate sequence according to their respective ordinal values. 3.2 Numerals shall precede letters of the alphabet. This is equivalent to saying that 9 shall precede A. Examples 1 Book 6 books 9 books 54 books Agriculture Applecart
NOTE -- It is recommended that the method of writing entries should be so standardized that numbers are always written as Hindu-Arabic numerals and not as Roman numerals or in words. The unhelpful order, to which the writing of numbers in words leads, is illustrated by the following example: a) eight books b) five books c) one hundred beoks -d) seven books e) six books

b)

2.2.4

The entries in language, other then English shall follow the English alphabetical usage except when the entries are all in a particular Indian or foreign In that case the language other than English. alphabetical usage of that particular language will be followed. 2.2.5 Diacritical Marks The letters or words with diacritical marks shall be ignored in alphabetization. But in giving the sequence between two entries or items with diacritical marks and without it, the item with the diacritical marks shall be written earlier to the one without it. 2.2.6 Cross-Reference Entries

4 SYMBOLS 4.1 Definition By `symbols' is meant non-alphabetical, numerals, internationally accepted characters, and signs used in particular subjects. 4.2 Symbols shall precede alphabets. 4.3 The symbols be spelled out and arrange them by their corresponding words in the language used. These will then be arranged in the sequence given in Annex A. 4.4 Other Symbols Symbols in any other subject shall be given ordinal values in such a way that they fall together; the assigning of ordinal values to the sets so formed shall be in conformity with the sequence of the subjects given in the Colon Classification given in Annex B. 4.4.1 The internal sequence among the symbols belonging to a subject shall be standardized as and when need arises. 5 ENTRIES IN DIFFE-RENT ALPHABETS nonmarks

There shall be cross-reference index entries from every alternative form of the entry word to every other. Exumples a) At the beginning as well as at the end of the block of entries beginning with `Saint', the following cross-reference should be inserted: For entries beginning with contractions of `Saint' and `Sainte', see entries beginning with `St' and `Sta'. b) Again, at the beginning and at the end of the block of entries beginning with `St' the following cross-reference should be inserted: For entries beginning with the uncontracted word or other contractions of it, see entries beginning with `Saint' and also `Sainte' and `Ste'. c) So also at the beginning and at the end of the block of entries beginning with `Ste' the following reference should be inserted: For entries beginning with the uncontracted word or other cont~~ctions of it, see entries beginning with `Sainte' and also `Saint' and `St'.

5.1 Entries in different alphabets shall be arranged in separate sequences. For example, the entries in Roman, Greek and Devnagari scripts shatl each form a sequence of its own separately. 5.2 The ordinal values of the characters of an alphabet shall be the same as in the language of the alphabet. For instance, in Roman script `a' shall precede `b'. 2
